calm.name: Calm
calm.key_insight: Calm's behavioral design challenge is philosophically interesting: can you ethically use behavioral science to help people build habits that may eliminate the need for your product? Calm's answer is content expansion — become a 'wellness platform' rather than a 'meditation app.' But this risks cognitive load creep as the product tries to be everything at once.

candy-crush.name: Candy Crush
candy-crush.key_insight: Candy Crush Saga has generated over $20 billion in lifetime revenue by perfecting a single behavioral loop: give players a sense of near-mastery, then introduce failure through randomness, then offer to sell the solution. This is not accidental — it's the direct application of Natasha Schull's 'machine zone' concept from casino design to mobile gaming. The game's levels are algorithmically tuned to produce a specific failure rate: too easy and players don't spend, too hard and they quit. The optimal frustration point — where players believe they 'almost had it' and one more try (or one purchased power-up) will succeed — is the core monetization engine. The lives system (5 lives, 30-minute regeneration) creates artificial scarcity of play itself, making continued play feel like a premium commodity. King's brilliance is making the monetization feel like the player's choice ('I choose to buy a power-up') rather than the system's design ('the level was tuned to make you fail without one'). Candy Crush is the purest distillation of free-to-play behavioral economics: the product is free, and frustration is the revenue model.
candy-crush.top_technique: Near-Miss Level Design as Monetization Engine
